Asymptotic Variance of the Semipartial (Part) Correlation Coefficient

Source: R/var_semipartial_r.R
var_semipartial_r.Rd

Computes a variance for the sample semipartial (also known as the part) correlation coefficient \(r_{Y(X \cdot Z_1 \cdots Z_{p-1})}\) under multivariate normality. The function provides two quantities, both of which need the full-model coefficient of multiple determination \(R^2_{Y \cdot X Z_1 \cdots Z_{p-1}}\): the squared standard error in the t test of \(X\)'s coefficient (the default when R2_full is supplied; Cohen, Cohen, West, & Aiken, 2003), and the first-order normal-theory variance of the sample semipartial correlation (under_null = FALSE), which is the quantity for a Wald confidence interval and for sample size planning. Without R2_full the function returns the first-order variance for the special case in which the variables partialed out explain none of the outcome, and warns.

Usage

var_semipartial_r(r_sp, N, p = 2, R2_full = NULL, under_null = TRUE)

Arguments

r_sp

Sample semipartial correlation coefficient \(r_{Y(X \cdot Z_1 \cdots Z_{p-1})}\), with the other variables partialed out of \(X\) only (not \(Y\)). Must be in \([-1, 1]\).

N

Total sample size.

p

Number of predictors in the regression of Y on X and the variables partialed out, so p - 1 variables are partialed out and p is at least 2. A categorical variable with a levels counts as a - 1 predictors. It is the p of ss_power_R2, ci_R2, and ci_reg_coef: the correlation concerns one predictor of a regression with p predictors. In the notation of a model comparison, \(q\) is the number of predictors removed from the full model to give the restricted model (\(q = p_{full} - p_{restricted}\), the predictors being tested), and the number of variables partialed out is \(p - q\); this correlation concerns one predictor, so \(q = 1\) and \(p - 1\) variables are partialed out. Defaults to 2 (one variable partialed out).

R2_full

Coefficient of multiple determination \(R^2_{Y \cdot X Z_1 \cdots Z_{p-1}}\) from the full model that includes \(X\) and every variable partialed out (R2_Y_X in ci_reg_coef; the squared semipartial correlation is R2_full minus the squared multiple correlation of the model without X). Must be in \([0, 1]\) and cannot be smaller than r_sp squared, because the squared semipartial correlation is the part of the full-model \(R^2\) that \(X\) adds; a smaller value is refused with an error of class dmar_semipartial_r_incoherent, unless the two values could have come from rounding to two decimals (see Details). When NULL (the default), the value returned is the first-order variance that holds when the variables partialed out explain none of the outcome, with a warning of class dmar_semipartial_r_no_R2_full.

under_null

Logical, used only when R2_full is supplied. If TRUE (the default), the function returns \((1 - R^2)/(N - p - 1)\), the squared standard error in the t test of \(X\)'s coefficient. If FALSE, it returns the first-order normal-theory variance of the sample semipartial correlation, evaluated at r_sp and R2_full.

Value

A one-row data.frame with columns term (either "var_semipartial_r" or "var_semipartial_r_under_null") and value (the requested variance).

Details

Background. The squared semipartial \(r^2_{Y(X \cdot Z)}\) equals the increase in \(R^2\) when \(X\) is added to a model already containing the variables partialed out, \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_{p-1}\), that is, the unique variance in \(Y\) attributable to \(X\). Unlike the partial, the semipartial is on the original scale of \(Y\) rather than on the partialed scale, which makes it the natural effect size companion to standardized regression coefficients in multiple regression reports (Cohen et al., 2003). Aloe and Becker (2012) propose it as an effect size for regression predictors in meta-analysis. ss_power_R2_change plans the power of the test of that change in \(R^2\).

First-order variance (under_null = FALSE). Write \(\rho_{sp}\) for the population semipartial correlation, \(P^2\) for the population full-model squared multiple correlation, and \(P_r^2 = P^2 - \rho_{sp}^2\), the squared multiple correlation of \(Y\) with \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_{p-1}\) alone. Under multivariate normality, to first order in \(1/N\), $$N\,\mathrm{Var}(\hat r_{sp}) \;\to\; (1 - \rho_{sp}^2)^2 \;-\; P_r^2\,(1 - 2 \rho_{sp}^2).$$ The variance depends on the population through \(\rho_{sp}\) and \(P_r^2\) only. Three cases show how it behaves. When the variables partialed out explain none of the outcome (\(P_r^2 = 0\)) it is \((1 - \rho_{sp}^2)^2\), the form of a simple or partial correlation. When \(\rho_{sp} = 0\) it is \(1 - P^2\). For \(P_r^2 > 0\), it is smaller than \((1 - \rho_{sp}^2)^2\) when \(\rho_{sp}^2 < 1/2\) and larger when \(\rho_{sp}^2 > 1/2\). Because the variance depends on \(P_r^2\), no function of \(r_{sp}\) alone stabilizes it, and Fisher's Z transformation does not apply to a semipartial correlation as it does to a partial correlation. The expression is the first-order variance of Aloe and Becker (2012, Equation 4), which they obtain from Alf and Graf (1999), with \(N - p\) in place of their \(n\): their numerator, \(P^4 - 2 P^2 + P_{(f)}^2 + 1 - P_{(f)}^4\) with \(P_{(f)}^2\) the squared multiple correlation of the model without \(X\), equals the expression above with \(P_r^2 = P_{(f)}^2\). The result follows from the delta method variance of the difference between two nested squared multiple correlations (Model A of Olkin & Finn, 1995, for one variable partialed out; Alf & Graf, 1999, for any number), because \(r_{sp}^2\) is that difference and so \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat r_{sp}) \approx \mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\Delta R^2}) / (4 \rho_{sp}^2)\).

The function evaluates the expression at r_sp and R2_full and divides by \(N - p\). The number of variables partialed out does not enter the first-order variance. The divisor \(N - p\) is a convention, kept for agreement with var_partial_r and because, with estimated values, a Wald interval formed with it has coverage closer to the nominal level than one formed with \(N\); it is not the most accurate estimate of the variance itself (in simulation neither \(N - 1\) nor \(N - p\) was closer to the observed variance in every condition).

The approximation has limits that simulation shows and that no theory given here corrects: it understates the variance when \(|\rho_{sp}|\) is large and \(N - p\) is small (in one simulated condition, \(\rho_{sp} = .95\), \(P_r^2 = 0\), \(p = 2\), and \(N = 40\), it was about 39 percent of the variance observed), and the sample semipartial correlation is biased toward zero by roughly \(\rho_{sp} (p - 1) / (2N)\). A Wald interval formed from it also misses the population value too often when the full-model \(R^2\) is near 1 and \(N\) is small, for any \(\rho_{sp}\) (in one simulated condition, \(\rho_{sp} = .1\), a full-model \(R^2\) of .99, \(p = 4\), and \(N = 12\), it missed in .13 of samples). When \(|\rho_{sp}|\) is above about .9 and the variables partialed out explain some of the outcome, the interval misses more often on one side than the other even with several hundred observations (in one simulated condition, \(\rho_{sp} = .95\), a full-model \(R^2\) of .97, \(p = 2\), and \(N = 395\), it missed in .064 of samples, .051 of them on one side).

Values rounded to two decimals. Reported values are often rounded, and a rounded pair can have R2_full slightly below r_sp squared: a semipartial correlation reported as .46 has a square of .2116, and the full-model \(R^2\) beside it may be reported as .21. When R2_full + .005 is at least \((|r_{sp}| - .005)^2\) (with the difference in parentheses not below 0), the pair is consistent with rounding. The function then gives a warning of class dmar_semipartial_r_rounded, which carries the two values, and proceeds: the squared semipartial correlation cannot exceed the full-model \(R^2\), so the variables partialed out are taken to explain none of the outcome (\(P_r^2 = 0\)) in the first-order variance, and the squared standard error of the t test uses R2_full as given. A pair further apart than rounding allows is refused. ss_aipe_semipartial_r and ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity apply the same rule to their values.

Without R2_full. The function returns \((1 - r_{sp}^2)^2 / (N - p)\), the first-order variance at \(P_r^2 = 0\). When the variables partialed out explain some of the outcome, this value is too large if \(\rho_{sp}^2 < 1/2\) and too small if \(\rho_{sp}^2 > 1/2\), which is why the call warns. At \(r_{sp} = 0\) it is \(1/(N - p)\) whatever the full-model \(R^2\), where the first-order variance is \((1 - P^2)/N\).

Squared standard error of the t test (R2_full supplied, under_null = TRUE). In multiple regression the unique contribution of \(X\) is tested with $$F \;=\; \frac{r^2_{Y(X \cdot Z)}\,(N - p - 1)}{1 - R^2_{Y \cdot X Z}} \;\sim\; F(1,\, N - p - 1)$$ under \(H_0\!: \rho_{Y(X \cdot Z)} = 0\) (Cohen et al., 2003). Equivalently \(t = \hat r_{sp}\,\sqrt{(N - p - 1)/(1 - R^2_{Y \cdot X Z})}\) is a t-statistic on \(N - p - 1\) degrees of freedom, and the function returns the square of its denominator, $$\frac{1 - R^2_{Y \cdot X Z}}{N - p - 1},$$ the squared standard error in the t test of \(X\)'s coefficient. It uses the sample \(R^2\) and equals the first-order variance at \(\rho_{sp} = 0\); it is the ingredient for testing the significance of \(X\)'s unique contribution, not a variance for an interval about a nonzero \(r_{sp}\).

With under_null = TRUE the value is \((1 - R^2_{full})/(N - p - 1)\), which equals \(r_{sp}^2/t^2\) for the t statistic of the predictor's coefficient, by the identity \(r_{sp} = t\sqrt{(1 - R^2_{full})/(N - p - 1)}\) (Aloe & Becker, 2012, Equation 2).

References

Alf, E. F., Jr., & Graf, R. G. (1999). Asymptotic confidence limits for the difference between two squared multiple correlations: A simplified approach. Psychological Methods, 4(1), 70–75. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.4.1.70

Aloe, A. M., & Becker, B. J. (2012). An effect size for regression predictors in meta-analysis. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 37(2), 278–297. doi:10.3102/1076998610396901

Cohen, J., Cohen, P., West, S. G., & Aiken, L. S. (2003). Applied multiple regression/correlation analysis for the behavioral sciences (3rd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum.

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 4 on contrasts, Chapter 5 on multiple comparisons, and Chapter 9 on ANCOVA.)

Olkin, I., & Finn, J. D. (1995). Correlations redux. Psychological Bulletin, 118(1), 155–164. doi:10.1037/0033-2909.118.1.155

Examples

# First-order variance of a semipartial r = .25 with N = 100, three
#     variables partialed out of X (p = 4 predictors in the full model),
#     and a full-model R^2 of .42.
var_semipartial_r(r_sp = 0.25, N = 100, p = 4, R2_full = 0.42,
                  under_null = FALSE)
#>  term              value
#>  var_semipartial_r 0.006

# By default, with R^2 of the full model supplied, the function returns
#     the squared standard error in the t test of X's unique
#     contribution.
var_semipartial_r(r_sp = 0.25, N = 100, p = 4, R2_full = 0.42)
#>  term                         value
#>  var_semipartial_r_under_null 0.006

# A reported pair, r_sp = .46 with a full-model R^2 of .21, in which
#     rounding has left R^2 below .46^2 = .2116: the value is returned
#     with a warning that says how the pair was read. The handler keeps
#     the message and lets the call finish, so both are shown.
noted <- new.env()
rounded <- withCallingHandlers(
  var_semipartial_r(r_sp = 0.46, N = 100, p = 2, R2_full = 0.21),
  dmar_semipartial_r_rounded = function(w) {
    noted$message <- conditionMessage(w)
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  })
rounded
#>  term                         value
#>  var_semipartial_r_under_null 0.008
noted$message
#> [1] "'R2_full' (0.21) is below 'r_sp' squared (0.2116) by no more than rounding to two decimals allows. The squared semipartial correlation cannot exceed the full-model R2, so one of the two was rounded. The value returned does not depend on r_sp and uses R2_full as given."
